Since molluscum is self-limited, watchful waiting appears to be the best management option for mild, uncomplicated, non-genital cases. A
Topical treatments and surgical interventions do not appear to hasten resolution of non-genital molluscum in the short-term and are associated with adverse events. A

background.definition: Molluscum contagiosum is a common, self-limited cutaneous viral infection, characterized by dome-shaped umbilicated papules.

list.listitem: Overall incidence: 2.4/1000/year.
Children aged 0 to 14 years: incidence 13/1000/year.
Molluscum contagiosum is caused by a double-stranded DNA pox virus, of genus Molluscipoxvirus, and exists as four genetic subtypes, MCV-1, MCV-2, and the much rarer subtypes, MCV-3 and MCV-4.
It is transmitted by skin-to-skin contact.
The incubation period is 2 weeks to 2 months.
The epidermis and hair follicle infundibulum are colonized by MCV.
Specimens show intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies known as molluscum bodies, with a hypertrophied hyperplastic epidermis.
In sexually active adults, it is transmitted during sexual activity.
Cell-mediated immunity plays an important role in clearance.
Screen for other sexually transmitted diseases in patients with genital lesions. C
Consider HIV testing in patients presenting with extensive or large facial lesions. C
Typical appearance is single or multiple clusters of 2-5 mm, pearly, dome-shaped, waxy-appearing, umbilicated papules, with easily expressible cheesy material. C
Consider sexual abuse in a child when molluscum is found restricted to the genital area. C
Consider biopsy of large or atypical lesions and in patients with AIDS and multiple lesions if disseminated cryptococcosis is in the differential diagnosis. C

Differential.Differential_Features: No central umbilication, may occur on palms and soles
Surface telangiectasias, irregular growth, possible bleeding and ulceration
Central keratotic plug, rapid growth, scarring after resolution
No central umbilication, rough surface, narrow to wide projections on a broad base
Lesions often painful, may have prodromal symptoms, tender lymphadenopathy, positive Tzanck smear

list.listitem: Molluscum typically presents as single or multiple clusters of pearly dome-shaped, waxy-appearing papules 2 to 5 mm in diameter, often with central umbilication. Cheesy off-white material is easily expressed from lesions. Giant lesions can present up to 1.5 cm in diameter.

It usually presents on exposed sites including face, eyelids, neck, trunk, axilla, extremities, and anogenital area. It can also present on mucous membranes. It does not present on the palms or soles.
Patients are generally asymptomatic, but can present with mild pruritus, tenderness, surrounding eczema, or secondary impetiginization.
Case reports show that an inflammatory phenomenon which includes redness, swelling, and crusting often precedes disease resolution.

In adults, it is mostly found on lower abdomen and groin. HIV-infected individuals may present with multiple or giant lesions in the beard area or face, which persist from autoinoculation and may enlarge.
Consider sexual abuse in a child when molluscum is restricted to the genital area.
Molluscum may heal with postinflammatory pigmentary changes (i.e., hypo- or hyperpigmentation), especially in skin of color.
Molluscum infection may trigger an eczematous reaction around the papules or at distant sites known as a hypersensitivity or id reaction.
Consider biopsy in patients with AIDS and multiple lesions if disseminated cryptococcosis is in the differential.
Consider biopsy of large or atypical lesions.
Staining with Giemsa or Wright stain, after biopsy or expression of the central core, demonstrates the large inclusion bodies on direct microscopy.
Application of liquid nitrogen may accentuate the appearance of the central umbilication as a black dot with surrounding frozen white area, allowing easier visual diagnosis.

Diagnostic features on dermoscopy include central umbilication in association with polylobular white to yellowish amorphous structures, surrounded by linear, fine and blurred "corona"-like telangiectasias.
Awaiting spontaneous resolution appears to be the best management option, as the disease is self-limited and evidence for different treatment options is poor.A
Topical treatments and surgical interventions do not appear to hasten resolution of non-genital molluscum in the short-term and are associated with adverse events.A
Very limited evidence suggests treatment of genital molluscum using self-applied topical imiquimod or podophyllin may be effective, but local reactions are common. B
One small RCT showed similar resolution rates and significantly less scarring by physical expression of lesions, compared to piercing with a sharp orange stick impregnated with phenol.
Currently, there are no therapeutic treatments approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for molluscum contagiosum.
A case series of 300 children with nonfacial lesions showed benefit with topical cantharidin, with clearance of 90%, and an average number of treatments of 2.

A prospective double blind placebo controlled RCT including 94 children aged between 2 and 17 demonstrated 40% total clearance in catharidin with occlusion compared to 10% with placebo with no serious adverse events or side effects
Retrospective chart reviews show benefit of intralesional Candida antigen therapy in pediatric molluscum contagiosum.

A 2017 Cochrane review concluded topical treatments and surgical interventions for non-genital molluscum do not appear to hasten resolution of symptoms in the short-term and are associated with adverse events (e.g., pain, erythema, itching). The reviewed trials were limited by absence of blinding, high dropout rates, small study sizes, and failure to perform intention-to-treat analyses.

Topical imiquimod 5% appears no more effective than vehicle, based on moderate-quality evidence from 4 studies involving 850 participants in the short-term (12 weeks), medium-term (18 weeks), and long-term (28 weeks). Application site reactions occurred more in the imiquimoid group. Number needed to treat to harm (NNTH) for imiquimod to cause any site reaction was 11, while NNTH for severe application site reaction was >40.

Based on low-quality evidence, there appears to be limited evidence regarding the superiority and short-term efficacy of multiple comparisons. Cryotherapy and 10% potassium hydroxide (KOH) appear better 5% imiquimod. 10% Australian lemon myrtle oil seems better than olive oil. 10% benzoyl peroxide cream appears more effective than 0.05% tretinoin. 5% sodium nitrite with 5% salicylic acid seems better than 5% salicylic acid alone. Iodine with tea tree oil appears more effective than tea tree oil or iodine alone. 10% potassium hydroxide seems better saline. Homeopathic calcarea carbonica seems better than placebo. 5% potassium hydroxide appears better than 2.5% potassium hydroxide. 10% povidone iodine with 50% salicylic acid plaster seems better than salicylic acid plaster alone.

A 2019 RCT evaluating the topical treatment of molluscum in children 2 to 16 years-old showed that 10% KOH gel applied once daily for 30 days was better than placebo (55.3% vs 16.3%, p <0.001), but had higher adverse events (72.3% vs 31.8%, p <0.001).
Very limited evidence suggests treatment of genital molluscum using self-applied topical imiquimod or podophyllin may be effective, but local reactions are common.

Recent studies of berdazimer gel,10.3% whch is a novel topical, once daily, nitric oxide-releasing medication, showed favorable efficacy although benefit should be weighed against potential for topical adverse effects particularly in pediatric patients.

A 2023 systematic review and network meta-analysis showed ingenol mebutate (not available in US or Canada), cryotherapy, podophyllotoxin, and KOH were more effective than other interventions in achieving complete clearance, but safety concerns including carcinogenesis regarding ingenol mebutate have been reported. Another systematic review and network meta-analysis in 2023 showed higher complete clearance for ingenol mebutate, VP-102, salicylic acid & lactic acid, KOH 10%, curettage, KOH 15%, and SB206 12% compared to placebo. Ingenol mebutate was pulled out of the European market in 2020 for its association with higher rates of nonmelanoma skin cancer, and discontinued in the US in 2022.
There is insufficient evidence regarding the more commonly used treatments such as cryotherapy or curettage.
Surgical or mechanical treatment options include curettage, cryotherapy, electrical cautery, laser removal, pricking or physical expression.
A small study found that pretreatment with EMLA cream followed by physical expression was similarly effective and associated with less scarring than phenol.
A small RCT with 10% Australian lemon myrtle oil in children showed benefit compared to placebo by 21 days, with no adverse effects reported.
Another small double-blind RCT showed benefit of Melaleuca alternifolia (tea tree oil) with iodine compared to iodine alone at 30 days with no discontinuation of treatment due to adverse effects.
Molluscum contagiosum is self-limited; therapy is not necessary for recovery, and awaiting spontaneous resolution is an important option in management.

Low-quality evidence suggests that intralesional immunotherapies including candida, combined MMR vaccine, tuberculin purified protein derivative, and interferon alpha may be effective for molluscum, with minimal adverse effects. More rigorous studies are needed before these therapies become standard treatment options.

Spontaneous regression occurs in non-HIV infected individuals, generally without scarring, unless previously infected. It may take 6 months to 2-5 years for molluscum to disappear but spontaneous resolution is its natural history; the mean time to resolution is 13.3 months.C

For sexually-transmitted genital molluscum, there is no recommendation for contact tracing or need for follow-up, unless other diseases that require these are found. Patients with genital molluscum should be checked for other STDs. C
In patients with HIV, treating the underlying disease with highly active antiretroviral therapy improves the likelihood of resolution of lesions. C
Cover lesions, avoid close contact, avoid picking.
For genital molluscum, have sexual partners checked for lesions. There is a risk for reinoculation/transmission between sexual partners.
Towels, bed linen and clothes should not be shared when active lesions are present, to reduce risk of onward transmission.
Avoid shaving or scratching the lesional area to prevent autoinoculation and secondary infection.
Lesions should be covered with clothing or watertight bandages prior to contact sports or using swimming pools.
Topical cantharidin, imiquimod, podophyllin, tretinoin, and trichloroacetic acid should be avoided in pregnancy.
Cryotherapy or curettage are possible options, as is expectant management.
EMLA cream may be applied 60 to 90 minutes before physical treatments such as curettage or cryotherapy.
Consider sexual abuse in a child when molluscum is found restricted to the genital area.
